criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1 (wrong service). The paper empirically examines struggles over housing/land tenure (in Punjabi Basti, West Delhi, and Sectors 5 and 8, NOIDA) and electricity supply/metering (in Punjabi Basti), rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Water and sanitation appear only in brief descriptive remarks (p. S47 fn. 8 noting surveyed Punjabi Basti households used multiple water sources without analyzing other localities; p. S49 noting open drains and few toilets in NOIDA), and p. S52 fn. 18 explicitly states that ongoing projects for access to water and sewage disposal are left as an open question for now.
criterion_notes.c2: Under BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, no legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing water or sanitation service access is examined. Although the study analyzes rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms—including land/eviction litigation, unauthorized-colony address mapping required for utility metering, electricity privatization (BSES) and anti-theft enforcement, and official surveys and identity/residency documentation for resettlement housing eligibility—these mechanisms are analyzed exclusively in relation to housing and electricity, not water or sanitation. Consequently, both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3: empirical mixed-methods study drawing on ethnographic fieldwork and interviews (including 40 address-history interviews in Punjabi Basti and 40 in-depth household interviews on voting and political participation), court and organizational documents, and a random-sample survey of 1,200 households across four localities in Delhi and NOIDA.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4 for water and sanitation: the outcomes analyzed are housing tenure security, court stay orders against demolition, contested eligibility surveys for alternate housing allotment, and installation of electricity transformers and household electricity meters. Passing background remarks on multiple water sources in Punjabi Basti and scarce toilets/open drains in NOIDA are not analyzed as study outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: While the mixed-methods study design and settlement/household populations are identifiable for the housing and electricity case studies, no exposure-outcome relationship is identified or analyzed for water or sanitation service access.

study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study combining ethnographic interviews, court/documentary analysis, and a random-sample household survey
population_and_sample: Residents, households, and local leaders in two unplanned settlements in the National Capital Region of Delhi (Punjabi Basti in West Delhi, 2,318 plots; and shanty clusters in Sectors 5 and 8 of NOIDA, Uttar Pradesh), based on a random sample of 1,200 households across four localities and ethnographic interviews (including 40 address-history interviews and 40 household political-participation interviews)
exposure: Engagement with legal, bureaucratic, and utility rules governing housing and electricity (land/eviction litigation, municipal approval of an address map for electricity metering, BSES electricity privatization and theft enforcement, and administrative surveys and residency documentation for alternate housing); no water or sanitation exposure analyzed
outcome: Housing tenure security/eviction stay orders, disputed resettlement flat eligibility lists, and formal household electricity metering and transformer installation; no water or sanitation service access outcome analyzed
rationale: Excluded under E07 (Wrong service). Although this empirical ethnographic and survey study investigates how residents and local leaders in unplanned settlements in Delhi and NOIDA navigate courts, bureaucracy, residency/address documentation, and privatized utility rules, its substantive empirical analysis focuses exclusively on housing/land tenure and electricity metering. Water and sewage/sanitation are mentioned only as brief unanalyzed background details, and the authors explicitly state (p. S52, fn. 18) that ongoing projects for access to water and sewage disposal are left as an open question for now.
